# EIGRP Authentication

> **Level 11 · EIGRP** — CCNP Enterprise (ENCOR 350-401)

---

## 1. Overview

**EIGRP authentication** allows an EIGRP router to verify that received EIGRP packets were generated by a neighbor that possesses the configured authentication key.

It protects the EIGRP adjacency from unauthorized or incorrectly configured routing peers and helps prevent an attacker or accidental device from participating in the EIGRP domain.

EIGRP authentication is configured **per interface / address-family interface**, not per area.

EIGRP authentication can use different authentication mechanisms depending on the IOS/IOS XE platform and configuration mode, including:

- **MD5**
    
- **HMAC-SHA-256** in supported named-mode implementations
    

Authentication is **not enabled by default**.

### Core idea

```text
EIGRP packet
     ↓
Authentication information
     ↓
Neighbor verifies packet
     ↓
Valid → process packet
Invalid → reject packet
```

If two EIGRP neighbors are configured with incompatible authentication parameters, the EIGRP adjacency will not form correctly.

---

## 2. Authentication Methods

|Method|Security|Notes|
|---|---|---|
|None|None|Default; authentication disabled|
|MD5|Legacy message authentication|Common classic EIGRP authentication|
|HMAC-SHA-256|Stronger cryptographic authentication|Supported by modern IOS/IOS XE named EIGRP implementations|

### Important

Do not memorize:

> "EIGRP plaintext authentication is the normal authentication method."

For CCNP/ENCOR, focus primarily on:

```text
MD5
HMAC-SHA-256
key chains
```

The exact authentication algorithms available depend on the Cisco IOS/IOS XE release and platform.

---

## 3. What Authentication Protects

EIGRP authentication helps verify the **integrity and authenticity of EIGRP packets** between configured neighbors.

It helps prevent unauthorized devices from successfully participating in the EIGRP adjacency.

However:

> **EIGRP authentication does not encrypt the routing information.**

Authentication provides packet authentication/integrity; it does not provide confidentiality.

Therefore, authentication does **not** mean:

```text
EIGRP routing information is encrypted
```

Instead:

```text
EIGRP routing packet
        ↓
Authentication check
        ↓
Valid / invalid
```

---

## 4. Key Chains

Cisco key chains provide the keys used by authentication mechanisms.

Example:

```text
key chain EIGRP-KEYS
 key 1
  key-string SecretKey123
```

A key chain can contain multiple keys:

```text
key chain EIGRP-KEYS
 key 1
  key-string OldSecret
 key 2
  key-string NewSecret
```

Each key has a **key ID**.

The key ID allows EIGRP to identify which configured key is being used.

---

## 5. Key Lifetimes

Keys can have:

- **Send lifetime**
    
- **Accept lifetime**
    

Example:

```text
key chain EIGRP-KEYS
 key 1
  key-string OldSecret
  send-lifetime 00:00:00 1 January 2026 infinite
  accept-lifetime 00:00:00 1 January 2026 00:00:00 31 January 2026
```

The exact IOS syntax for lifetime configuration can vary, but the concept is the important part.

### Send lifetime

Controls when the router can use the key for **outgoing authenticated packets**.

### Accept lifetime

Controls when the router accepts packets authenticated with that key.

---

## 6. Key Rotation

Multiple keys can be configured so that authentication credentials can be changed without an outage.

Conceptually:

```text
Old Key
   │
   │ accept + send
   ↓
New Key introduced
   │
   │ accept + send
   ↓
Old Key expires
```

The important design principle is:

> **Ensure the old and new keys have an appropriate overlap period.**

This prevents a period where one side sends with a key that the other side is no longer accepting.

### Exam memory

```text
Key rotation
     ↓
Multiple keys
     ↓
Overlapping lifetimes
     ↓
No authentication gap
```

---

# 7. Classic EIGRP Authentication

Classic IPv4 EIGRP uses interface-level authentication commands.

### Step 1 — Create the key chain

```text
key chain EIGRP-KEYS
 key 1
  key-string SecretKey123
```

### Step 2 — Enable MD5 authentication

```text
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip authentication mode eigrp 100 md5
 ip authentication key-chain eigrp 100 EIGRP-KEYS
```

The important commands are:

```text
ip authentication mode eigrp <AS> md5
```

and:

```text
ip authentication key-chain eigrp <AS> <KEY-CHAIN>
```

Authentication must be configured consistently on the interfaces forming the EIGRP adjacency.

---

## 8. Named EIGRP Authentication

Named EIGRP places interface-specific authentication under:

```text
router eigrp <name>
 address-family ...
  af-interface <interface>
```

For example:

```text
key chain EIGRP-KEYS
 key 1
  key-string SecretKey123
  cryptographic-algorithm hmac-sha-256

router eigrp CAMPUS
 address-family ipv4 unicast autonomous-system 100
  af-interface GigabitEthernet0/1
   authentication mode hmac-sha-256
   authentication key-chain EIGRP-KEYS
  exit-af-interface
 exit-address-family
```

The important hierarchy is:

```text
router eigrp CAMPUS
    ↓
address-family ipv4
    ↓
af-interface
    ↓
authentication
```

### Applying authentication to all interfaces

Named EIGRP supports:

```text
af-interface default
```

This can be used to apply interface-specific EIGRP settings broadly.

Example:

```text
router eigrp CAMPUS
 address-family ipv4 unicast autonomous-system 100
  af-interface default
   authentication mode hmac-sha-256
   authentication key-chain EIGRP-KEYS
  exit-af-interface
 exit-address-family
```

This is useful when the same authentication configuration should apply to all EIGRP interfaces in the address family.

---

## 9. HMAC-SHA-256

**HMAC-SHA-256** provides stronger cryptographic authentication than legacy MD5.

A typical named-mode configuration uses a key chain:

```text
key chain EIGRP-KEYS
 key 1
  key-string SecretKey123
  cryptographic-algorithm hmac-sha-256
```

and associates that key chain with the EIGRP address-family interface:

```text
router eigrp CAMPUS
 address-family ipv4 unicast autonomous-system 100
  af-interface GigabitEthernet0/1
   authentication mode hmac-sha-256
   authentication key-chain EIGRP-KEYS
  exit-af-interface
 exit-address-family
```

### Important

Do not memorize:

> "HMAC-SHA-256 is automatically enabled in named mode."

It is **not** automatic.

You must configure authentication.

---

# 10. Authentication Must Match

For an EIGRP adjacency to form correctly, both neighbors must have compatible authentication configuration.

For example:

```text
R1                              R2

Algorithm: SHA-256              Algorithm: SHA-256
Key: Secret123                  Key: Secret123
Key chain: EIGRP-KEYS            Key chain: EIGRP-KEYS
        │                              │
        └──────── Authentication ──────┘
                     ✓
```

If the authentication parameters do not match:

```text
R1                              R2

Key: Secret123                  Key: WrongKey
        │                              │
        └──────── Authentication ──────┘
                     ✗
```

The EIGRP adjacency will fail to establish or remain operational.

---

# 11. Authentication Is Per Interface / AF

EIGRP does **not** have an OSPF-style area-wide authentication model.

Authentication is associated with the EIGRP interface/address-family configuration.

Conceptually:

```text
R1
 ├── Gi0/0 → EIGRP authentication
 ├── Gi0/1 → EIGRP authentication
 └── Gi0/2 → no authentication
```

Therefore, authentication can differ between EIGRP interfaces if the design requires it.

In named mode:

```text
address-family
    ↓
af-interface
    ↓
authentication
```

---

# 12. EIGRP IPv6 Authentication

EIGRP authentication concepts also apply to EIGRP for IPv6.

With named mode:

```text
router eigrp CAMPUS
 address-family ipv6 unicast autonomous-system 100
  af-interface GigabitEthernet0/1
   authentication mode hmac-sha-256
   authentication key-chain EIGRP-KEYS
  exit-af-interface
 exit-address-family
```

The key principle remains:

> Both EIGRP neighbors must use compatible authentication configuration.

---

# 13. Authentication vs Encryption

This is an important exam distinction.

### Authentication

Answers:

> **"Did this packet come from a peer that knows the secret, and has it been altered?"**

### Encryption

Answers:

> **"Can someone else read the packet contents?"**

EIGRP authentication provides the first function, not the second.

```text
Authentication
    ↓
Integrity / authenticity

Encryption
    ↓
Confidentiality
```

Therefore:

> **EIGRP authentication does not encrypt EIGRP routing updates.**

---

# 14. Troubleshooting

## 14.1 Neighbors Do Not Form

Check:

```text
show ip eigrp neighbors
```

If the expected neighbor is missing, verify:

```text
show ip eigrp interfaces detail
```

Then check:

- Authentication mode
    
- Key chain
    
- Key string
    
- Algorithm
    
- Key lifetime
    
- EIGRP AS
    
- Interface configuration
    

---

## 14.2 Authentication Failure

Common causes:

```text
Wrong key string
Wrong key ID
Wrong algorithm
Wrong key chain
Expired key
Send/accept lifetime mismatch
Authentication configured on only one side
```

---

## 14.3 Key Rotation Causes Adjacency Flaps

If authentication suddenly fails during a key change, check:

```text
show key chain
```

Look for:

- Current active key
    
- Send lifetime
    
- Accept lifetime
    
- Expired keys
    
- Missing overlap
    

A lifetime gap can cause packets to be rejected during the transition.

---

# 15. Verification Commands

### Key Chain

```text
show key chain
```

Displays configured key chains and their key/lifetime information.

---

### EIGRP Interfaces

Classic EIGRP:

```text
show ip eigrp interfaces detail
```

Useful for checking EIGRP interface configuration and authentication details.

---

### Neighbors

```text
show ip eigrp neighbors
```

If authentication is misconfigured, the expected neighbor may not appear.

---

### Running Configuration

```text
show running-config | section key chain
show running-config | section router eigrp
```

These commands help verify the actual configured key chain and EIGRP hierarchy.

---

# 16. Troubleshooting Workflow

Use this order:

```text
1. Check physical/interface state
        ↓
2. Verify EIGRP AS
        ↓
3. Verify EIGRP is enabled on the interface
        ↓
4. Verify authentication is enabled consistently
        ↓
5. Verify authentication algorithm
        ↓
6. Verify key chain
        ↓
7. Verify key string
        ↓
8. Verify key ID
        ↓
9. Verify send/accept lifetimes
        ↓
10. Check neighbor table
```

This prevents wasting time debugging routing when the actual problem is authentication.

---

# 17. Common Failures

|Symptom|Likely Cause|Check|
|---|---|---|
|Neighbor never appears|Authentication mismatch|Compare both sides|
|Neighbor disappears after key change|Lifetime problem|`show key chain`|
|Authenticated packets rejected|Wrong key/string|Check key chain|
|Authentication mismatch|Different algorithm|Check MD5 vs SHA-256|
|One side authenticates|Authentication enabled on only one side|Configure both sides|
|Adjacency flaps periodically|Key lifetime/rotation issue|Check send/accept lifetimes|
|Named-mode authentication not working|Wrong configuration hierarchy|Check `af-interface`|
|Authentication works on one link but not another|Per-interface configuration difference|Check each AF interface|

---

# 18. Exam Traps

### Trap 1 — Authentication is not enabled by default

EIGRP normally operates without authentication unless you configure it.

---

### Trap 2 — Authentication does not encrypt EIGRP

```text
Authentication ≠ Encryption
```

It provides packet authentication/integrity, not confidentiality.

---

### Trap 3 — HMAC-SHA-256 is configured, not automatic

Do not assume named mode automatically enables SHA-256.

You still need:

```text
authentication mode hmac-sha-256
```

and the appropriate key chain.

---

### Trap 4 — Key chain is not the same thing as authentication

A key chain stores the authentication keys.

EIGRP must be configured to **use** the key chain.

Conceptually:

```text
Key chain
   ↓
Stores keys
   ↓
EIGRP authentication
   ↓
Uses the keys
```

---

### Trap 5 — Authentication is per interface / AF

There is no EIGRP "area authentication" concept like OSPF areas.

Named mode:

```text
address-family
    ↓
af-interface
    ↓
authentication
```

---

### Trap 6 — Both neighbors must agree

Authentication parameters must be compatible on both ends of the EIGRP adjacency.

If one router uses:

```text
HMAC-SHA-256
```

and the other expects:

```text
MD5
```

the authentication will fail.

---

### Trap 7 — Key rotation requires careful lifetimes

Remember:

```text
send-lifetime
accept-lifetime
```

A properly planned overlap allows the old and new keys to coexist during the transition.

---

|Purpose|Authenticate EIGRP packets|
|Encryption|**No**|

|Modern method|HMAC-SHA-256 where supported|

|Key identifier|Key ID|

|Rotation|Overlapping lifetimes|

|Classic IPv4|`ip authentication mode eigrp`|
|Classic key chain|`ip authentication key-chain eigrp`|
|Named mode|`af-interface`|
|Named algorithm|`authentication mode hmac-sha-256`|
|Named key chain|`authentication key-chain`|
|Apply to all AF interfaces|`af-interface default`|
|Verification|`show key chain`|
|Neighbor verification|`show ip eigrp neighbors`|
|Interface verification|`show ip eigrp interfaces detail`|
|Mismatch|Adjacency fails|

# 20. One-Minute Mental Model

Think of EIGRP authentication as:

```text
                 EIGRP Neighbor
                       │
                       │
                EIGRP Packet
                       │
                       ↓
              Authentication Check
                       │
              ┌────────┴────────┐
              │                 │
           Valid             Invalid
              │                 │
              ↓                 ↓
       Process packet      Reject packet
```

The configuration hierarchy is:

```text
Classic:

key chain
    ↓
interface
    ↓
ip authentication mode eigrp
ip authentication key-chain eigrp
```

Named mode:

```text
key chain
    ↓
router eigrp NAME
    ↓
address-family
    ↓
af-interface
    ↓
authentication
```

### Core ENCOR formula

> **EIGRP Authentication = Key Chain + Authentication Algorithm + EIGRP Interface/AF Configuration + Matching Parameters on Both Neighbors**

### Key commands to remember

```text
key chain EIGRP-KEYS
 key 1
  key-string SecretKey123
  cryptographic-algorithm hmac-sha-256
```

```text
router eigrp CAMPUS
 address-family ipv4 unicast autonomous-system 100
  af-interface GigabitEthernet0/1
   authentication mode hmac-sha-256
   authentication key-chain EIGRP-KEYS
  exit-af-interface
 exit-address-family
```

And for classic EIGRP:

```text
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip authentication mode eigrp 100 md5
 ip authentication key-chain eigrp 100 EIGRP-KEYS
```
